case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Fair Credit Reporting Act’s civil-liability provisions unmistakably waive the United States’ sovereign immunity so that federal agencies can be sued for damages for willful or negligent FCRA violations.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA), 15 U.S.C. §§ 1681n (willful noncompliance civil liability), 1681o (negligent noncompliance civil liability), and the definitional provision 15 U.S.C. § 1681a(b) (defining “person” to include any “government or governmental subdivision or agency”); plus the federal sovereign-immunity clear-statement rule (waivers must be unequivocal and unambiguous).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The USDA Rural Housing Service argues that §§ 1681n and 1681o do not unequivocally and unambiguously waive federal sovereign immunity. Even though the FCRA defines “person” to include “any … government,” that definition should not be read to expose the United States to private damages actions because waivers must be unmistakably clear and reading “person” to include the federal government throughout the statute produces implausible consequences (e.g., punitive damages, criminal liability, or certain enforcement mechanisms applied to the government). The government also points to the FCRA’s structure and surrounding statutory context (including other privacy-related schemes) to argue Congress did not clearly choose to subject federal agencies to FCRA damages.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Kirtz argues the waiver is explicit in the statute’s text: §§ 1681n and 1681o impose civil liability on “any person,” and § 1681a(b) expressly defines “person” to include “any … government or governmental subdivision or agency,” which encompasses federal agencies. Under ordinary textual interpretation, that combination satisfies the clear-statement rule. Potential awkwardness in applying the definition to other FCRA provisions (punitive damages, criminal provisions, enforcement sections) is not a basis to override clear text; courts can apply the definition as written absent a truly exceptional reason (e.g., constitutional problems or genuine absurdity). Congressional silence in legislative history cannot defeat an express statutory definition.
key_precedents: Return Mail, Inc. v. U.S. Postal Service, 139 S. Ct. 1853 (2019)
Kimel v. Florida Board of Regents, 528 U.S. 62 (2000)
Robinson v. Department of Education, 917 F.3d 799 (4th Cir. 2019) (cert. denied, 140 S. Ct. 1440 (2020) (Thomas, J., dissenting))
Daniel v. National Park Service, 891 F.3d 762 (9th Cir. 2018)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito rightly stress Lane v. Peña’s unmistakable-clarity requirement and Return Mail’s caution that a generic “person” definition may not suffice to impose monetary burdens on the sovereign, particularly given the punitive-damages implications of § 1681n. But Return Mail itself hinged on the absence of an express definition; here § 1681a(b) expressly defines “person” to include “any … government,” and §§ 1681n–1681o then use that defined term (“any person”) to trigger civil liability—textual linkage that, under my minimalist approach, is hard to label genuinely ambiguous without effectively nullifying Congress’s definition. The proper institutional response to the Government’s anomaly concerns is to decide only the threshold question (the United States is a proper defendant under §§ 1681n–1681o) and leave remedy-limiting questions—especially punitive damages—open for a later case, rather than manufacturing ambiguity at the waiver stage. Justice Kagan’s provision-by-provision approach best preserves both precedent and judicial restraint while respecting the enacted text.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice rely on § 1681a(b)’s definition of “person” to include “any … government” and argue that, when §§ 1681n–1681o impose damages on “any person,” the waiver is unequivocal. But under Lane v. Peña and FAA v. Cooper, the question is not whether “government” appears somewhere in a definitional section; it is whether Congress unmistakably subjected the United States to private money damages (and especially punitive damages) in the liability provisions themselves, and the FCRA’s structure and remedial anomalies make that inference at least doubtful. Return Mail does not merely ask whether a definition exists; it reflects the deeper rule that general terms and global definitions are not enough to do the heavy work of waiving sovereign immunity for damages absent a clear, tailored statement directed to federal liability. The Chief Justice’s suggested “narrow holding” that treats the United States as a proper defendant while potentially carving back remedies confirms the ambiguity rather than curing it, because it requires courts to selectively disable the definition’s ordinary cross-subchapter effect to avoid consequences the text does not clearly authorize against the sovereign.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan (and the Chief) rely on Return Mail’s statement that the sovereign-excluding presumption falls away where Congress supplies an express definition, and § 1681a(b)’s inclusion of “any … government” is certainly strong evidence. But Lane v. Peña demands an unequivocal waiver of money-damages liability as to the United States, and I do not think a global definitional hook—especially one that would also carry punitive damages under § 1681n—meets that tailored clear-statement requirement when the overall remedial scheme creates serious structural doubt about Congress’s intent. Chief Justice Roberts’ proposed “narrow holding” limited to §§ 1681n–1681o underscores the problem: it effectively asks us to treat the same defined term as sovereign-including here but not elsewhere, which is not faithful to how subchapter-wide definitions work and is itself a sign of ambiguity to be resolved in the Government’s favor. Return Mail thus remains a cautionary guide: absent a waiver that speaks directly to federal damages liability, we should not infer it from a broad definition that produces anomalous consequences.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s best point—that Lane v. Peña and FAA v. Cooper require an “unmistakable” money-damages waiver and that punitive-damages exposure under § 1681n makes the scheme suspect—does not overcome the fact that Congress expressly defined “person” to include “any … government” in § 1681a(b). As Justice Kagan emphasizes, Return Mail’s presumption that “person” excludes the sovereign operates only “in the absence of an express statutory definition,” and here the civil-liability provisions use the defined term “any person,” which is the ordinary, unequivocal drafting mechanism Congress uses to make governments suable. To the extent punitive damages or other remedies raise special sovereign-immunity concerns, I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that those issues can be handled narrowly and provision-by-provision without erasing the threshold waiver in §§ 1681n–1681o. Given the FCRA’s consumer-protection purpose and the real harms from federal credit-reporting errors, I do not see genuine statutory ambiguity that would justify denying a damages remedy altogether.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s best point is that Lane v. Peña demands an unmistakable waiver for money damages and that punitive-damages exposure under § 1681n looks anomalous. But the waiver question here is textual: §§ 1681n–1681o impose liability on “any person,” and § 1681a(b) expressly defines “person” to include “any … government,” which (as Chief Justice Roberts notes) is the kind of definition-plus-liability linkage Return Mail treats as dispositive when present. The “anomalies” argument goes to remedy scope and workability, not to whether Congress unmistakably included the Government in the class of liable defendants where it used the defined term; we can address punitive damages (if necessary) by strict construction of that remedy rather than by nullifying the definition in the threshold liability provisions. Under my pragmatic textualism, the most coherent course is Roberts’s cabined holding recognizing the United States as a proper defendant under §§ 1681n–1681o while reserving harder remedial questions for cases that squarely present them.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito rightly emphasize that waivers of sovereign immunity must be unmistakable and that reading the United States as a “person” can generate awkward remedial consequences (notably punitive damages). But under Lane v. Peña the question is whether the waiver is unequivocally expressed in the statutory text, and here Congress did the usual textualist work: §§ 1681n–1681o impose liability on “any person,” and § 1681a(b) expressly defines “person” to include “any … government,” the very circumstance Return Mail said would change the analysis “in the absence of an express statutory definition.” Chief Justice Roberts’ suggestion to keep the holding cabined to the civil-liability provisions is consistent with applying the definition where it is used while leaving remedy-specific questions (including punitive damages) to be strictly construed if and when they are squarely presented. The “anomalies” argument may inform provision-by-provision construction, but it cannot manufacture ambiguity in a defined term that Congress directly linked to the liability provisions.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito are right to press that Lane v. Peña demands an unequivocal waiver for money damages and that reading “person” to include the United States can generate awkward consequences, especially punitive-damages exposure under § 1681n. But Return Mail, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, treated the sovereign-excluding presumption as operating “in the absence of an express statutory definition,” and here § 1681a(b) expressly defines “person” to include “any … government,” which is the standard textual mechanism Congress uses to make liability provisions like §§ 1681n–1681o apply to government actors. The practical anomalies do not create ambiguity in the threshold waiver where Congress used a defined term that expressly includes the sovereign; the more institutionally cautious course is to apply the waiver where the definition is incorporated, while leaving remedy-specific questions (including punitive damages) to strict construction in an appropriate case rather than erasing the waiver altogether. That approach respects precedent, Congress’s drafting choices, and the Court’s legitimacy by deciding no more than necessary.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s and Justice Alito’s best point—grounded in Lane v. Peña and FAA v. Cooper—is that any residual ambiguity about money damages (especially punitive damages under § 1681n) must be resolved for the sovereign, and they read Return Mail to require something more tailored than a definition. But Return Mail itself draws its presumption “in the absence of an express statutory definition,” and § 1681a(b)’s definition of “person” to include “any … government or governmental subdivision or agency” is precisely the kind of textual clarity that, under a textualist methodology, controls the meaning of “any person” in §§ 1681n–1681o. The Government’s anomaly concerns are real, yet they go to the scope of particular remedies (and invite strict construction of punitive damages) rather than erasing the threshold waiver Congress wrote via a defined term. Chief Justice Roberts’s suggestion of a narrow holding limited to the civil-liability provisions best aligns with honoring the definition where used while avoiding unnecessary pronouncements about other sections.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito press the most serious challenge: Lane v. Peña demands an unmistakable money-damages waiver and, they argue, a definitional inclusion of “any … government” is too generic to do that work given punitive-damages and other structural anomalies. But Return Mail’s core distinction—emphasized by Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice—is that the presumption against treating the sovereign as a “person” yields when Congress supplies an express definition, and § 1681a(b)’s subchapter-wide definition coupled with §§ 1681n–1681o’s “any person” liability is about as direct a textual waiver as we are going to get. On my pragmatic, fairness-focused approach, we should not manufacture ambiguity to deny a damages remedy for concrete harms from federal credit-reporting errors; instead, as the Chief Justice suggests, courts can address remedy-specific overbreadth (including punitive damages) via strict construction if and when it arises. That approach respects the text while managing practical consequences without nullifying Congress’s definitional choice.

John Roberts.reasoning: Sections 1681n and 1681o impose damages liability on “any person,” and Congress expressly defined “person” in § 1681a(b) to include “any … government or governmental subdivision or agency,” which on its face reaches federal agencies. Under Lane v. Peña, a waiver must be “unequivocally expressed” in statutory text and legislative history cannot supply (or defeat) a waiver; here, the definitional provision supplies the necessary textual clarity for civil liability. While the Government’s concerns about awkward applications elsewhere in the FCRA warrant a cautious, provision-by-provision reading, they do not create sufficient ambiguity in §§ 1681n–1681o to override Congress’s express definition. A narrow holding recognizing a waiver only for the FCRA’s civil-liability provisions best respects precedent and institutional legitimacy without extending beyond the text.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under the sovereign-immunity clear-statement rule, Congress must waive the United States’ immunity for money damages in unequivocal statutory text, and any ambiguity must be resolved in favor of immunity. Lane v. Peña, 518 U.S. 187, 192 (1996); FAA v. Cooper, 566 U.S. 284, 290–291 (2012). Although 15 U.S.C. §§ 1681n and 1681o impose liability on “any person” and § 1681a(b) defines “person” to include a “government,” that general definitional move does not unmistakably and unambiguously expose the United States to private damages (including punitive damages under § 1681n) given the serious structural and contextual indications that “person” is not meant to carry that meaning throughout the Act. Consistent with Return Mail, Inc. v. U.S. Postal Serv., 139 S. Ct. 1853 (2019), where a general definition did not suffice to subject the Federal Government to burdens absent a clear textual statement directed to the United States, I would hold the FCRA lacks an unmistakable waiver and thus preserves sovereign immunity here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under the clear-statement rule, a waiver of federal sovereign immunity for money damages must be “unequivocally expressed” and any ambiguity must be resolved in favor of immunity. Lane v. Peña, 518 U.S. 187, 192 (1996). Although §§ 1681n and 1681o impose liability on “any person” and § 1681a(b) defines “person” to include “any … government,” that definitional move does not unmistakably and unambiguously subject the United States to private damages actions, given the serious practical and structural anomalies that follow if the Government is treated as a “person” across the Act (including punitive-damages exposure under § 1681n and other enforcement provisions). Consistent with Return Mail, Inc. v. U.S. Postal Serv., 139 S. Ct. 1853 (2019), I would not read a general definition to work a sovereign-immunity waiver absent a clear, tailored statement that Congress meant to authorize damages suits against federal agencies.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Sections 1681n and 1681o impose damages liability on “any person,” and Congress expressly defined “person” in § 1681a(b) to include “any … government or governmental subdivision or agency,” which on its face encompasses federal agencies and satisfies the clear-statement rule for waiving sovereign immunity. Under Lane v. Peña, waivers must be unequivocal, but they can be established through the interaction of broad remedial language with provisions making the Government subject to the statute’s requirements; here, Congress both subjected government actors to FCRA duties and then authorized suits for willful or negligent noncompliance by “any person.” The government’s “implausible consequences” arguments do not create ambiguity in §§ 1681n/1681o’s damages remedy, because courts can apply § 1681a(b)’s definition to the civil-liability provisions without extending it to distinct criminal or enforcement provisions in a way that would be genuinely absurd. Given the FCRA’s consumer-protection purpose and the real-world harms of inaccurate credit reporting—often borne most heavily by vulnerable borrowers—reading the statute to provide a damages remedy against federal agencies best fits Congress’s chosen text and ensures meaningful access to justice.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Sections 1681n and 1681o impose damages liability on “any person,” and Congress expressly defined “person” for purposes of the entire FCRA subchapter to include “any … government or governmental subdivision or agency,” 15 U.S.C. § 1681a(b), which straightforwardly encompasses federal agencies. Under the clear-statement rule, the question is whether the waiver is “unequivocally expressed” in statutory text, Lane v. Peña, 518 U.S. 187 (1996), and this combination of an all-encompassing liability trigger (“any person”) plus an explicit definition including government is about as clear as Congress can be. Return Mail reinforces that the usual presumption that “person” excludes the sovereign applies only “in the absence of an express statutory definition,” 139 S. Ct. at 1861–62; here there is one, and workability concerns about other FCRA provisions do not justify rewriting the definition rather than applying ordinary tools to resolve any genuine conflicts provision-by-provision. Because the text unmistakably brings federal agencies within the civil-liability provisions, sovereign immunity is waived for those damages actions.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The question is whether Congress spoke with the requisite clarity to subject the United States to FCRA damages, and the statute’s text does so: §§ 1681n and 1681o authorize civil actions against “any person,” while § 1681a(b) expressly defines “person” to include “any … government or governmental subdivision or agency.” Under Lane v. Peña, a waiver must be “unequivocally expressed in statutory text,” and this definitional cross-reference supplies that clear statement without resort to implication or legislative history. The government’s parade of awkward applications elsewhere in the Act cannot override a definition Congress supplied for the whole statute; at most, such concerns go to the scope of particular remedies or provisions, not to negating the waiver where the remedial sections expressly incorporate the defined term. Return Mail’s caution against assuming the sovereign is a “person” absent clear indication cuts the other way here because Congress provided exactly that indication in § 1681a(b).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Sections 1681n and 1681o impose damages liability on “any person,” and Congress expressly defined “person” to include “any … government or governmental subdivision or agency,” 15 U.S.C. § 1681a(b), which is the kind of clear textual linkage that ordinarily satisfies the sovereign-immunity clear-statement rule. Under Lane v. Peña, waivers must be “unequivocally expressed in statutory text,” but that standard is met when the liability provisions incorporate a definition that unmistakably reaches governmental entities, and a court should not create ambiguity by speculating about awkward applications elsewhere in the statute. Return Mail is distinguishable because there the term “person” lacked the same direct definitional clarity reaching the Federal Government in the relevant provision, whereas here Congress wrote an explicit definition and used the defined term in the damages sections. Practical concerns about punitive damages or other provisions can be handled by narrowing the remedy consistent with strict construction, but they do not justify denying the threshold waiver for suit under §§ 1681n and 1681o.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Sections 1681n and 1681o impose damages liability on “any person” for willful or negligent noncompliance, and the FCRA’s definitional provision expressly provides that “person” includes “any … government or governmental subdivision or agency,” 15 U.S.C. § 1681a(b); reading these provisions together supplies the “unequivocal” textual waiver the clear-statement rule demands. Under Lane v. Peña, waivers must be “unambiguous,” and here Congress used an express definition that, by its ordinary public meaning, encompasses federal agencies. Return Mail confirms that the presumption that “person” excludes the sovereign applies “in the absence of an express statutory definition,” but where Congress defines the term, that definition controls. Potential awkward applications elsewhere in the Act are not enough to override the clear text in §§ 1681n–1681o as applied to federal agencies’ civil liability.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Sections 1681n and 1681o impose damages liability on “any person,” and Congress expressly defined “person” in § 1681a(b) to include “any … government or governmental subdivision or agency,” which on its face encompasses federal agencies; that is the kind of textual clarity the clear-statement rule demands. Under Lane v. Peña, waivers must be unequivocal, but courts do not manufacture ambiguity where Congress has supplied an explicit definition that, when applied to the liability provisions, authorizes suit for willful or negligent noncompliance. The government’s policy concerns about punitive damages or awkward applications elsewhere are better handled through provision-specific interpretation rather than rewriting the definition, and practical consequences favor allowing individuals harmed by federal credit-reporting errors a meaningful damages remedy consistent with FCRA’s consumer-protection aims.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Fair Credit Reporting Act’s civil-liability provisions, which impose liability on “any person” and define “person” to include “any ... government or governmental subdivision or agency,” clearly and unambiguously waive the United States’ sovereign immunity so that federal agencies can be sued for damages for FCRA violations.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA), 15 U.S.C. §§ 1681n (willful noncompliance civil liability), 1681o (negligent noncompliance civil liability), and 1681a(b) (definition of “person” including “any ... government or governmental subdivision or agency”); plus the federal sovereign-immunity clear-statement canon (waivers must be “unequivocally expressed” in statutory text).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: USDA Rural Housing Service argues that Congress did not “unequivocally and unambiguously” waive federal sovereign immunity in FCRA’s damages provisions. Even though FCRA defines “person” to include “government,” USDA contends that reading “person” in §§ 1681n and 1681o to include the United States would produce implausible consequences across the statute (e.g., punitive damages, criminal liability, and enforcement mechanisms that are awkward or nonsensical if applied to the federal government). USDA also points to the demanding nature of the sovereign-immunity clear-statement rule and argues that Congress typically uses more explicit language when it intends to expose the federal government to private damages suits; therefore, the generic “any person” formulation is insufficient to waive immunity.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Kirtz argues that the statute’s text already supplies the required clear statement: §§ 1681n and 1681o impose civil liability on “any person,” and § 1681a(b) expressly defines “person” to include “any ... government or governmental subdivision or agency,” which necessarily includes federal agencies. Under standard interpretive rules, that express definition controls absent an exceptional reason. Concerns about punitive damages, criminal provisions, or other applications do not justify overriding clear text because definitions can be context-limited where necessary (e.g., to avoid absurdity or constitutional problems) without nullifying the waiver in the civil-liability sections. Kirtz also disputes reliance on legislative silence or policy concerns as a basis to defeat an otherwise clear textual waiver.

Return Mail, Inc. v. U.S. Postal Service, 587 U.S. 16 (2019)
Robinson v. Department of Education (cert. denied), 140 S. Ct. 1440 (2020) (Thomas, J., dissenting from denial of certiorari)
Daniel v. National Park Service, 891 F.3d 762 (9th Cir. 2018)
Robinson v. Department of Education, 917 F.3d 799 (4th Cir. 2019)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s structural-anomaly point (especially punitive damages) is the best argument for the Petitioner, but it goes to remedy-scope and context, not to whether Congress made the waiver clear in the first place. Lane v. Peña asks for an unequivocal textual expression, and §§1681n and 1681o impose liability on “any person” while §1681a(b) expressly defines “person” to include “any … government or governmental subdivision or agency,” which is the clearest kind of textual hook Return Mail found missing. As Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, our ordinary way to avoid overbreadth is context-sensitive application of definitions and, where appropriate, narrow construction of particular remedies—rather than nullifying an explicit definitional inclusion across the board. Institutionally, the sound course is a narrow holding limited to waiver for damages actions under §§1681n and 1681o, leaving any harder applications of “person” elsewhere in FCRA for future cases.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that extending §1681a(b)’s definition of “person” into §§1681n and 1681o yields contextual anomalies—especially punitive damages—that, he argues, reveal ambiguity defeating an “unequivocal” waiver under Lane v. Peña and Return Mail. But Lane’s clear-statement rule is satisfied by enacted text that directly answers the coverage question, and here Congress expressly defined “person” to include “any … government or governmental subdivision or agency,” which §§1681n and 1681o then apply to “any person.” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Return Mail cautions against implying the sovereign’s inclusion from silence; it does not authorize us to disregard an explicit statutory definition, and any remedial overbreadth can be handled provision-by-provision (including narrowing punitive damages against the sovereign if the text and our remedial canons require it) rather than rewriting “government” out of §1681a(b). On originalist and textualist grounds, the Government’s policy intuitions about punitive damages cannot override Congress’s clear words that encompass governmental entities in the liability-triggering term.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kagan press the hardest point: §§1681n and 1681o impose liability on “any person,” and §1681a(b) defines “person” to include “any … government,” which looks like the Lane v. Peña clear statement. But Lane requires an unequivocal waiver as to the sovereign, and I do not think a global definitional clause—when mechanically imported—clearly commits the United States to punitive damages and other remedial features that Congress ordinarily addresses expressly; those remedial anomalies are not peripheral, they reveal ambiguity about whether Congress meant to subject the federal government to private damages suits at all. Return Mail reinforces that we should not treat “person” as including the sovereign absent unmistakable contextual fit, and here the mismatch between standard sovereign-immunity practice and the statute’s remedial scheme makes the asserted waiver less than unequivocal. I therefore would read “person” contextually in §§1681n and 1681o not to include the United States absent a more explicit waiver directed to federal agencies and the remedies available against them.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s concern that a definitional cross-reference could “silently” expose the United States to punitive damages is the best pushback, but it goes to remedial scope, not to whether Congress clearly included “any … government” within “person” for §§1681n and 1681o. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, our ordinary tools—context-sensitive application of definitions and narrow construction of remedies against the sovereign—address the punitive-damages worry without rewriting §1681a(b)’s explicit inclusion out of the statute. Lane v. Peña requires textual clarity, and the text here is unusually direct: the liability provisions apply to “any person,” and Congress defined that term to include government agencies, unlike the silence that drove Return Mail. A contrary reading would strip FCRA’s enforcement mechanism from individuals harmed by federal credit-reporting errors, with the predictable real-world effect of leaving the most vulnerable without a meaningful damages remedy.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s contextual-anomaly/punitive-damages point is the best pushback, but under Lane v. Peña the question is whether Congress clearly spoke in the enacted text, and §1681a(b)’s definition expressly including “any … government or governmental subdivision or agency” supplies that clarity for §§1681n and 1681o. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, the way to handle awkward consequences is context-sensitive application of definitions and, where appropriate, narrower construction of remedies—not treating those consequences as retroactively erasing an explicit definitional inclusion. Return Mail, which Justice Alito invokes, helps the Government only when the statute is silent or relies on background presumptions about “person”; it does not authorize us to disregard Congress’s own definition that directly answers the coverage question here. I therefore remain comfortable recognizing the waiver for these civil-liability provisions while leaving any remedial edge cases to provision-by-provision analysis.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is that applying §1681a(b)’s definition of “person” to §§1681n and 1681o may produce remedial oddities—especially punitive damages—that, he argues, defeat Lane v. Peña’s clear-statement requirement. But Lane asks whether Congress clearly expressed a waiver in the enacted text, and here Congress expressly defined “person” to include “any … government or governmental subdivision or agency,” then imposed liability on “any person”; that is not an implied waiver of the sort Return Mail cautions against. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan note, the proper textualist move is to apply the definition to the civil-liability provisions before us while addressing any genuinely ill-fitting remedial applications through ordinary context-sensitive interpretation (including potentially construing particular remedies narrowly as applied to the sovereign), rather than excising “government” from the statutory definition. Because Alito’s anomalies argument goes to downstream scope, not to whether the definitional cross-reference supplies clear coverage for these sections, I remain with the Respondent.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that punitive-damages exposure and other remedial “anomalies” suggest Congress did not waive immunity “unequivocally” under Lane v. Peña, and he invokes Return Mail to argue we should read “person” contextually to exclude the United States. But Lane’s clear-statement inquiry is satisfied where Congress itself defines the liability-triggering term—here §§1681n and 1681o apply to “any person,” and §1681a(b) expressly includes “any … government or governmental subdivision or agency,” which is the kind of direct textual hook Return Mail found missing. As Chief Justice Roberts suggests, the institutional and legally orthodox approach is a narrow holding that the definition controls for the civil-liability provisions before us, while leaving any genuinely ill-fitting remedial questions (including punitive damages) to provision-by-provision, context-sensitive treatment rather than nullifying the explicit definition. I therefore do not think the asserted anomalies convert clear text into ambiguity sufficient to defeat a waiver.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that the punitive-damages consequence makes the waiver insufficiently “unequivocal” under Lane v. Peña, but Lane asks whether Congress clearly expressed the waiver in the statutory text—and §§1681n and 1681o impose liability on “any person,” with §1681a(b) expressly defining “person” to include “any … government or governmental subdivision or agency.” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, contextual anomalies are ordinarily addressed by applying definitions with sensitivity to context, not by disregarding an explicit definitional inclusion that directly answers the coverage question in the provisions before us. Return Mail helps the Government only where the statute is silent or relies on ordinary usage; it does not justify excising “government” from Congress’s own definition. I therefore see no textual ambiguity in applying the definition to these civil-liability sections, even if remedial scope questions (like punitive damages) may require separate, narrower analysis.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s punitive-damages anomaly point is the best pushback, but under Lane v. Peña the question is whether Congress clearly spoke in the enacted text—and §1681a(b) expressly defines “person” to include “any … government or governmental subdivision or agency,” which §§1681n and 1681o then use to impose civil liability on “any person.” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, contextual awkwardness is handled by provision-by-provision interpretation (including narrowing particular remedies against the sovereign if warranted), not by effectively rewriting “government” out of the definition where it supplies the clear statement. Return Mail, as Justice Gorsuch notes, is about not inferring sovereign coverage from silence; here Congress provided the missing textual hook, so the waiver for these civil-liability provisions is not “implied” but incorporated by explicit definition. Given the FCRA’s remedial design and the practical need for a meaningful remedy when federal agencies mishandle credit information, I do not see Alito’s structural concerns as creating the kind of genuine ambiguity that would justify denying the waiver altogether.

John Roberts.reasoning: Sections 1681n and 1681o impose damages liability on “any person,” and Congress expressly defined “person” in § 1681a(b) to include “any … government or governmental subdivision or agency,” which is the kind of textual clarity our sovereign-immunity cases require when a waiver is “unequivocally expressed.” Lane v. Peña, 518 U.S. 187, 192 (1996). While the Government’s concerns about other FCRA provisions (e.g., punitive damages or criminal liability) are substantial, they can be handled through ordinary context-sensitive application of statutory definitions rather than overriding the definition wholesale, consistent with our approach in Return Mail, Inc. v. U.S. Postal Serv., 587 U.S. 16 (2019). A narrow holding recognizing a waiver only for the civil-liability provisions at issue best respects the enacted text while avoiding broader institutional disruption.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The sovereign-immunity clear-statement rule requires that any waiver be “unequivocally expressed” in the statutory text, Lane v. Peña, 518 U.S. 187 (1996). Here, the FCRA’s civil-liability provisions impose damages liability on “any person,” 15 U.S.C. §§ 1681n, 1681o, and Congress expressly defined “person” to include “any … government or governmental subdivision or agency,” § 1681a(b), which by its ordinary public meaning encompasses federal agencies. Applying that definition to §§ 1681n and 1681o yields a clear, textual waiver for those provisions, and speculative difficulties elsewhere in the statute do not permit rewriting an unambiguous definition or narrowing “any person” contrary to the enacted text. Because the waiver is stated in the statute itself through an express definitional clause, it satisfies Lane’s demand for clarity as to damages liability.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: A waiver of the United States’ sovereign immunity must be “unequivocally expressed” in the statutory text, and ambiguities are construed in the Government’s favor. Lane v. Peña, 518 U.S. 187 (1996). Although FCRA defines “person” to include “any … government or governmental subdivision or agency,” 15 U.S.C. § 1681a(b), reading that definition wholesale into §§ 1681n and 1681o would create serious contextual anomalies—most notably exposing the United States to punitive damages and other enforcement mechanisms that are ill-suited to the sovereign—casting doubt on any purportedly “unambiguous” waiver. Consistent with Return Mail, Inc. v. U.S. Postal Serv., 587 U.S. 16 (2019), the better reading is that “person” does not clearly include the Federal Government for purposes of private damages actions absent a more explicit statement from Congress.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: FCRA’s civil-liability provisions impose damages liability on “any person,” 15 U.S.C. §§ 1681n, 1681o, and Congress expressly defined “person” to include “any … government or governmental subdivision or agency,” § 1681a(b); that is the kind of textual clarity the sovereign-immunity clear-statement rule demands. Lane v. Peña requires an “unequivocal” waiver in the statutory text, but it does not authorize courts to disregard an explicit definition that directly answers who may be sued for damages. The government’s parade of consequences (punitive damages, criminal provisions, awkward enforcement) can be handled through ordinary context-sensitive reading and anti-absurdity principles without nullifying the waiver in §§ 1681n and 1681o. Denying a damages remedy here would undercut FCRA’s core purpose of ensuring accurate credit reporting and would leave individuals—often those least able to absorb the consequences of credit errors—without meaningful redress against federal agencies.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Sections 1681n and 1681o impose damages liability on “any person,” and Congress then defined “person” to include “any ... government or governmental subdivision or agency,” 15 U.S.C. § 1681a(b); under ordinary textual rules, that explicit definition supplies the requisite clear statement for a waiver as applied to federal agencies. The sovereign-immunity canon demands an “unequivocally expressed” waiver, but it does not permit courts to disregard a directly applicable statutory definition simply because other FCRA provisions might be awkward if applied to the United States; context-limited readings can address those provisions without nullifying the damages waiver. Lane v. Peña confirms that broad remedial language coupled with other provisions subjecting federal agencies to the statute can satisfy the clear-statement rule for money damages. Reading the civil-liability provisions to cover federal agencies is also the most workable, coherent way to align FCRA’s substantive duties (which apply to governmental actors) with its enforcement mechanism.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Sections 1681n and 1681o impose civil liability on “any person,” and Congress supplied an express, controlling definition in § 1681a(b) stating that “person” includes “any … government or governmental subdivision or agency,” which on its face encompasses federal agencies; that is the sort of textual clarity the clear-statement rule demands. Lane v. Peña requires waivers be “unequivocally expressed” and ambiguities resolved in favor of immunity, but here the statutory definition directly answers the immunity question for these civil-liability provisions. Concerns about awkward applications elsewhere in the FCRA do not justify rewriting the damages provisions; at most they may warrant context-specific limits on “person” in other sections without negating the waiver where Congress spoke expressly. Return Mail’s reluctance to read “person” to include the United States absent clear indication is satisfied here by the explicit definitional inclusion of “government” in § 1681a(b).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Sections 1681n and 1681o impose damages liability on “any person,” and Congress expressly defined “person” in § 1681a(b) to include “any … government or governmental subdivision or agency,” which is a strong textual clear statement that encompasses federal agencies. Under Lane v. Peña, waivers must be “unequivocally expressed” and ambiguities construed in favor of immunity, but here the operative liability term is expressly defined in the statute itself, leaving little room to read “person” to exclude the federal government. USDA’s concerns about awkward applications elsewhere in the FCRA (e.g., punitive or criminal provisions) do not justify overriding the statute’s controlling definition, and context-based narrowing can address any genuine absurdities without nullifying the waiver in §§ 1681n and 1681o. Return Mail’s caution about treating “person” to include the sovereign absent a clear statement is satisfied here because Congress did not leave the question to implication—it wrote the government into the definition of the term that triggers civil liability.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Sections 1681n and 1681o impose damages liability on “any person,” and Congress expressly defined “person” in §1681a(b) to include “any … government or governmental subdivision or agency,” which, as a textual matter, encompasses federal agencies. Under Lane v. Peña, a waiver must be “unequivocally expressed” in the statutory text, and here the definitional cross-reference supplies the requisite clarity rather than leaving the Government’s liability to implication. USDA’s concerns about awkward applications elsewhere in the FCRA do not create ambiguity in these civil-liability provisions; as in Sturgeon v. Frost, courts apply statutory definitions unless context requires otherwise, and any context-based narrowing can be handled provision by provision without negating the clear inclusion of government in §§1681n and 1681o. Strict construction may limit the waiver’s scope, but it does not permit rewriting “any … government” out of §1681a(b) where Congress chose to define the operative term broadly.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Sections 1681n and 1681o impose civil liability on “any person,” and Congress expressly defined “person” in § 1681a(b) to include “any … government or governmental subdivision or agency,” which is the kind of textual clarity the sovereign-immunity clear-statement rule demands. Lane v. Peña requires that waivers be “unequivocally expressed” and that ambiguities be resolved in favor of immunity, but here the operative liability provisions incorporate a definition that on its face reaches governmental agencies, including federal ones. USDA’s concerns about awkward applications elsewhere in FCRA do not justify nullifying an otherwise explicit waiver in the damages provisions; as in Sturgeon v. Frost, courts can read statutory terms in a context-sensitive way to avoid truly absurd results without rewriting the core civil-liability text. As a practical matter, allowing damages actions against federal agencies for credit-reporting misconduct promotes procedural fairness and accountability in a domain that directly affects access to housing and basic economic opportunity.
